item.description:

Short Description:
Map attack paths to your crown jewels (Crown Jewel → Attack Surface → Attack Vector), prioritize them with a configurable risk score and measure detection coverage by MITRE ATT&CK technique using Splunk ES correlation searches or your own detection inventory. Lookup-driven, with sample data included.


Description:
Attack Path Intelligence shows how an attacker could reach your organization's most critical assets, and whether your detections would catch them. The app models attack paths as Crown Jewel → Attack Surface → Attack Vector. Each path gets a priority score based on the crown jewel's criticality, the jewel-surface relationship, the vector's relevance, the surface's exposure and the evidence level. The evidence level says whether a vector was observed in logs, confirmed by a vulnerability scanner or only inferred from the architecture. Every vector is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and the app matches those techniques against your detections. You can use Splunk Enterprise Security correlation searches, read through their MITRE annotations, or a detection inventory lookup for rules outside ES. The result is a coverage view per vector, per path and per crown jewel. It also gives you a ranked detection engineering backlog and a list of disabled detections that would increase coverage if enabled. Optional live panels use the CIM Network_Traffic and Web data models to show real activity against the assets of each attack surface. Everything is lookup-driven and configurable: scores, weights, risk thresholds, MITRE match weights, data sources and CIM fields. The app ships with sample content for a fictional organization, so you can explore the dashboards before modeling your own environment.

item.title: Cloudflare Audit Logs Addon for Splunk - v1.1.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
Please provide a read-only API token for the Cloudflare account whose audit logs Splunk will collect. Grant Account / Account Settings / Read, and limit the account resource to the specific account. Supply its Account ID and send the token through our approved secret-sharing channel. If client-IP filtering is enabled, allow the actual outbound IPs of our Splunk collector. No write permission or Global API Key is requested." WHY THIS PERMISSION This TA calls GET /client/v4/accounts/{account_id}/audit_logs. The endpoint lists Account Settings Read or Account Settings Write as accepted permissions. Choose Read for least privilege; Write is not necessary for this integration. Source: Cloudflare's account audit log API reference: [https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/audit_logs/methods/list/](https://developers.cloudflare.com/api/resources/audit_logs/methods/list/) Do not substitute Access: Audit Logs Read. That permission covers Cloudflare Access authentication logs, not the account audit endpoint used here. Zone / Logs / Read and Logpush permissions are not required for this TA's request. Permission definitions: [https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/reference/permissions/](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/reference/permissions/) TOKEN SETUP 1\. An authorized Cloudflare user opens My Profile > API Tokens > Create Token and creates a custom token. Token creation does not give that user access to accounts or privileges they did not already have. 2\. Set policy type Account, permission Account Settings, access Read. 3\. Limit Account Resources to the account(s) authorized for collection. Prefer a dedicated token scoped to the single account for each input. 4\. Choose an expiry/rotation policy. If IP filtering is used, allow the actual collector egress IPs. The Splunk Web hostname's DNS address is not evidence of its outbound/NAT IP. Obtain Cloud egress information from your Splunk administrator or support team. 5\. Store the displayed secret securely. Enter it directly in the TA's Bearer Token field. Do not include "Bearer ", quotes or surrounding whitespace. 6\. Use the 32-character Account ID, not a Zone ID or account display name. Cloudflare also offers account-owned tokens. Use them only after confirming support for this endpoint and your organization's token-creation policy. Neither a Cloudflare password nor a Global API Key is accepted by this TA. Instructions and resource scoping: [https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/get-started/create-token/](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/api/get-started/create-token/) VALIDATE THE ACTUAL ACCESS Saving the Splunk form validates its format and securely stores the token; it is not proof that Cloudflare authorized retrieval. Enable one input and check for "Cloudflare poll completed" in the internal logs. HTTP 200 with success\=true and result\=\[] means no records were returned. HTTP 401/403 means the credential/access checks above still need review. Token validity alone does not prove permission to the requested account. This release uses the v1 account endpoint, not the separate v2 /logs/audit, organization audit-log or Zero Trust Access authentication-log APIs.


Description:
Cloudflare Audit Logs TA for Splunk is designed to integrate with your Cloudflare Cloud audit logs with the Splunk platform. This add-on focuses on data monitoring, enabling you to bring Cloudflare activities into Splunk in real-time.

item.title: Insights Suite for Splunk (IS4S) - v1.4.8 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
### 1.4.8 (November 20, 2026) **New features and improvements** * **Run now:** collections with scheduled searches offer Run now on the activation page, which starts every search right away instead of waiting for its next scheduled run. It asks you to confirm first and warns that running every search at once uses search resources and can slow other searches and dashboards during peak hours. The collection's schedule does not change. * **Value Impact Assistant on its own:** Value Impact Assistant is now its own collection that you can activate on its own or alongside Value Insights. Its Value Insights menu item appears once it is activated. * **Clearer search usage:** IS4S ties each search to the indexes and sourcetypes it names and counts every search run, so usage figures agree across KPIs. Use Case Insights shows matching sourcetypes again, with its details drill-down restored. * **User Insights:** User Insights searches have plain-language descriptions with guidance on reading their results, and the regularly seen and new-user counts are corrected. "Daily Trend of Regularly Seen Users" is now "Daily Trend of Active Users". **Bug fixes** * **Searches no longer get stuck after upgrading to 1.4.7:** IS4S releases a search slot at once when Splunk refuses the connection, stops waiting for searches that Splunk cancelled, releases expired slots held by other users, and releases uncertain starts after about 17 minutes. A run that has to wait says why in ssef.log, and a cancelled | ssef run stops within about 20 seconds instead of holding its check. * **Queued searches keep their place:** a search slot held by another user's search that is still queued or running is no longer released early, so the concurrency limit holds. * **Troubleshooting page works again:** lookup updates keep every column the lookup declares, so the Splunk instance lookup keeps its guid column and the troubleshooting dashboard loads. If you removed guid from a local copy of the ssef_instance_info(1) macro, delete that copy after upgrading. * **Lookup updates use far less memory:** while IS4S replaced a lookup, the check that guards the update held about nine times the lookup's size in memory (a 29 MB lookup took about 330 MB, and several updates at once added up). It now sends the lookup from a temporary file, so one update of that lookup peaks at about 90 MB. The lookup that results is unchanged. * **A deactivated collection stays deactivated:** when another collection still used a collection's searches, Deactivate changed nothing and the collection still showed as activated. IS4S now remembers the choice for each collection, so the collection list, the activation page, the manager and the wizard agree. * **Scheduled export:** export no longer leaves a KPI search running when checking its status fails. * **Alerts Failing to Trigger:** the card shows Normal when no alerts failed, and states how many hours were captured when capture is incomplete. * **Screen reader announcements:** screen readers announce when Run now starts and finishes, including on collections that are only partly scheduled. * **Activation page after a reload:** while a run continues after the page is reloaded, the badge shows its progress and Activate stays unavailable until the run ends. **Security** * Updated the bundled fast-xml-parser dependency to 5.12.0 for a published advisory. **Upgrade notes** * The troubleshooting page can still show the guid error right after the upgrade. An upgrade does not rewrite lookups, so the page recovers when the next scheduled run of a collection's checks updates the Splunk instance lookup.


Short Description:
Understand and maximize the value of your Splunk investment. IS4S runs curated search collections on a schedule, delivering continuous visibility into usage, adoption, performance, and analytic-capability attainment through executive-ready dashboards and in-app guidance. Works standalone; pairs with the Searchbase App to build custom collections.

item.title: DIA Data Integrity App - v2.0.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
2.0.1 \- New page layout: the Overview shows only the key numbers, four charts and the source inventory. \- New Mapping & Parsing page with tstats verification, CIM index macros, recommendations, parsing quality and ingestion warnings (moved from the Overview). \- The p90 job run time panel and the data models that are not measured moved to Setup & Health. \- Charts on every page; long tables side by side with 10 rows per page.


Description:
DIA Data Integrity App gives Splunk and data administrators detailed control panels for one question: is the data in every index and sourcetype correct and usable by CIM-based content such as correlation searches, dashboards and Splunk Enterprise Security? Data model mapping, verified: for 28 CIM data models the app runs tstats by index and sourcetype and records which sources really land in each data model. The verdict comes from tstats, not from CIM index macros or tags alone. Acceleration coverage and cim_*_indexes macros are checked too. CIM field profile: for every data model and source the app samples events and measures each CIM field - how often it is filled, how often it only holds placeholders such as unknown or -, and whether its values follow the CIM definition (expected values, number type, port, IP, hash and MAC shapes). Recommended fields that a source never fills are listed per source. Field definitions are read from the data models installed on your search head, so custom models and newer CIM versions are covered automatically. Field anomalies: every extracted field of every source is checked for broken names (generic CEF cs1/cn1 fields with their real name suggested from the label, positional field3 names, values used as field names, case-variant duplicates), malformed values (key=value inside a value, leftover quotes, spaces, unparsed JSON/XML, encoding artefacts), mixed number/text types, mostly empty fields and timestamp fields that cannot be parsed or disagree with _time. Parsing and time: unparsed and partially parsed sources, multi-line and future-dated events, indexing latency and likely time zone offsets. Recommendations for unmapped sources suggest the data model, tags, key CIM fields and the add-on to use. No setup is needed: after install, first-run searches build the analysis automatically within minutes and scheduled searches refresh it every 4 hours. Defaults are light (7 days, acceleration summaries only, 200-300 sampled events per source); every window, sample size and limit is a macro, and the Overview shows the p90 run time of each job with tuning recommendations. The app is read-only for your data and never changes props, transforms, data models or macros.

Host audit records (esx.audit.*): SSH or shell enabled and disabled, firewall changes, password changes, account lockouts. - Alerts: host problems (esx.problem.*), account lockouts and repeated login failures. - Web: requests to the host's web services from other machines (envoy-access): method, path, status, bytes, duration, client, TLS version, SOAP action. Also parses more than 100 ESXi processes: header (process, pid, log level, message), the [Originator@6876 sub= opID= user=] block, and process-specific fields: vmkernel modules, storage devices and latency, VM names and actions, HA (Fdm) state, VpxLRO operations, cron and SSH commands, VIB checks, Active Directory messages, etcd and cluster agent fields. Search-time only: install on search heads. Works with ESXi 7 and 8 layouts, classic or ISO timestamps, RFC 3164 or RFC 5424, with or without the syslog header. Short Description:
Collects Linux hwmon (lm-sensors class) board health - CPU/core temperatures, fans, voltages, NVMe temps, power - from BMC-less hosts with zero dependencies. Stdlib python3 reads /sys/class/hwmon and emits JSON events, mstats-ready sensors.* metrics, and dashboards.


Description:
TA-sensors brings hardware health monitoring to the machines IPMI can't reach. Consumer desktops, gaming rigs, VMs, SBCs and other BMC-less hosts have no out-of-band management controller, so server-grade hardware telemetry (temperatures, fans, voltages, power) is invisible to Splunk. The Linux kernel already exposes all of it through the hwmon subsystem under /sys/class/hwmon - TA-sensors collects it natively, without a BMC, without ipmitool, and without even the lm-sensors package. Two stdlib-only python3 scripted inputs collect every registered hwmon chip (coretemp/k10temp, acpitz, nvme, r8169, mt7921, amdgpu, vendor drivers, and more): - sensors:status (index=main): one nested-JSON event per cycle with sensor_name, reading, reading_value, units and status for every sensor, including latched _alarm flags. - sensors:metrics (index=metrics): true metric events via METRIC-SCHEMA, named sensors._, ideal for mstats time-series, anomaly alerts and trend dashboards. Milli-scaled sysfs inputs are normalized (temp/in/power/current/humidity /1000, fan raw rpm), duplicate chip names are disambiguated with their hwmon number, and all names are sanitized so metric names stay clean and dashboard-safe. Included dashboards: Sensors Overview (per-host reporting, current readings, alarm table) and Sensors Metrics (CPU cores, temperatures, fans, voltages, power draw, live metric volume). TA-sensors is fully standalone, but pairs with TA-IPMI, which covers BMC-equipped servers - together they give complete hardware observability across a mixed fleet. Free and source-available for personal, educational and evaluation use; commercial use requires a paid license from BentleyPC LLC (see LICENSE).

Description:
The Secutec SecureSight Add-on for Splunk collects your organization's assets and threats through the SecureSight Customer API. The Assets input indexes the asset inventory, including assets that were removed. The Threats input indexes every threat with its status, severity, CVSS score and the affected asset. The first run indexes the current state of every asset and threat; after that, a checkpoint makes sure each run only indexes what changed, such as a new threat or a status change, and that nothing is indexed twice or lost after an outage. Consume Apache Kafka, Amazon MSK and Confluent Cloud topics directly into Splunk Cloud Platform or Splunk Enterprise. No Kafka Connect, nothing installed on the Kafka side. SASL/SCRAM, TLS/mTLS, SOCKS5 proxy, consumer group offsets.


Description:
Collecting Kafka topics into Splunk usually requires running and maintaining a separate Kafka Connect cluster, which is not always possible. This add-on removes that intermediary: Splunk itself consumes the topics directly from Apache Kafka, Amazon MSK or Confluent Cloud, with nothing to install on the Kafka side. The add-on connects with SASL_SSL (SCRAM-SHA-512 for Amazon MSK, SCRAM-SHA-256, PLAIN for Confluent Cloud) or TLS/mTLS, supports private certificate authorities and an optional SOCKS5 proxy. Offsets are committed to a standard Kafka consumer group only after events are written to Splunk, giving at-least-once delivery and a consumer lag visible with the usual Kafka tools. A2Z Python Upgrade finds and fixes the Python 3.13, jQuery 3.5 and Splunk Cloud (AppInspect) blockers in every app installed on your Splunk platform. Many installed apps, especially unmaintained ones, are no longer compatible. The app scans all installed apps (and, on Splunk Enterprise, deployment server, cluster manager and SHC deployer apps) against 34 rules, explains every finding in plain English with the related AppInspect check, and generates a patched package with all safe fixes applied: python.required, splunklib upgrade, removed Python APIs, Simple XML version 1.1, bundled jQuery, packaging issues. item.title: OTel Fleet Monitor for AWS - v1.2.0 [New App Release]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
**1.2.0 — First public release on Splunkbase.** Features \- Inventory of OpenTelemetry Collectors on Amazon EKS and ECS through read-only AWS APIs (ECS, EKS, SSM, STS) and the read-only Kubernetes API of each EKS cluster: DaemonSets, Deployments, StatefulSets, pods, ConfigMaps, OpenTelemetryCollector custom resources and EKS add-ons (ADOT). Clusters without any collector are reported. \- Health: silent collectors (running on AWS but not reporting), dropped data by stage, signal and component, exporter sending-queue saturation. \- Versions: CURRENT / OUTDATED / OBSOLETE / UNSUPPORTED / UNPINNED status per workload, based on a version policy fed by GitHub releases and AWS DescribeAddonVersions. \- Expected vs applied configuration: rules per account, cluster, namespace or workload (version, config hash, required or forbidden components), detection of instances still running an older configuration, best-practice findings including plaintext secrets. \- 9 dashboards (including a Home page with a quick-start guide), 9 alerts shipped disabled, KV store reference data. \- Outbound proxy support: per input, app-wide (Administration > Proxy page, Splunk Cloud friendly), Splunk system proxy or environment variables. Proxy password and AWS secret key are stored encrypted in storage/passwords and masked. **Notes** \- Internal versions 1.0.0 and 1.1.0 were never published on Splunkbase. \- All AWS and Kubernetes calls are read-only. Python 3.7 to 3.14 compatible (Splunk Enterprise 9.x and 10.x, Splunk Cloud Platform).


Short Description:
Inventory, health and configuration drift for OpenTelemetry Collectors on Amazon EKS and ECS, directly in Splunk Platform. Finds silent collectors, dropped telemetry, outdated versions, plaintext secrets and differences between expected and applied collector configuration.


Description:
OpenTelemetry Collectors are now the backbone of telemetry pipelines on AWS, but most teams cannot answer basic questions about their own fleet: How many collectors run on EKS and ECS? Which ones stopped sending data? Which ones drop spans, metrics or logs? Which versions are outdated? Is the configuration that actually runs the one we expect? OTel Fleet Monitor for AWS answers these questions in Splunk Platform (Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud Platform), without requiring Splunk Observability Cloud. 1. Inventory A modular input calls read-only AWS APIs (ECS, EKS, SSM, STS) and the read-only Kubernetes API of each EKS cluster to discover every collector: ECS services and tasks, DaemonSets, Deployments, StatefulSets, pods, ConfigMaps, OpenTelemetryCollector custom resources and EKS add-ons such as ADOT. Clusters without any collector are reported. 2. Health The inventory is cross-checked with the collector internal telemetry (otelcol_* metrics): - Silent collectors: running on AWS but no longer reporting (SILENT, NEVER_REPORTED, NOT_INVENTORIED). - Dropped data: refused, dropped and failed-to-export items by stage, signal and component, plus exporter sending-queue saturation. - Versions: CURRENT, OUTDATED, OBSOLETE, UNSUPPORTED or UNPINNED (latest tag), based on a version policy fed by GitHub releases and on AWS add-on versions. 3. Expected vs applied configuration Define expected rules (version, config hash, required or forbidden components) per account, cluster, namespace or workload. The app compares them with the configuration really applied, detects instances still running an older configuration (previous task definition revision, pods started before the last ConfigMap change) and flags bad practices such as a missing memory_limiter, disabled retry or sending queue, disabled TLS verification and plaintext secrets. Included: 8 dashboards, 9 alerts (shipped disabled), KV store reference data, outbound proxy support. All AWS and Kubernetes calls are read-only; secrets are stored encrypted in Splunk and never indexed.

item.description:

Release Notes:
\- The field map tool generates maps for Windows Security as classic text (\`WinEventLog:Security\`), FortiGate and Palo Alto Networks, beside Windows Security as rendered XML and CloudTrail. With a FortiGate map, the Network_Traffic data model, \`tstats\` and the Splunk Security Content (ESCU) detections give the same results as on raw events. With a Palo Alto map, the Network_Traffic and Change data models, \`tstats\` and ESCU detections give the same results on compact PAN-OS traffic and system events as on raw ones; threat events are passed whole. \- The field map's \`check\` also counts the compact events indexed without their fields and those Splunk dropped because it could not load the map's lookup file, and fails with the count. When its probe arrives late, \`check\` keeps the template list unless Splunk's log shows events of the map dropped. The new Field Map Dropped Events alert reports dropped events by node every five minutes. \- The new search report, \`bin/tenx_search_report.py\`, reads a search head's saved searches, alerts and dashboards and says which run unchanged when a source moves to compact events, which need \`tx\`, \`txf\` or a field map, and which meet a limit the README states. The report changes nothing and starts no search. \- Word searches through \`tx\`, dashboards and compiled alerts find the events of every stored template, including templates stored in the last few minutes. Outside \`NOT\`, a wildcard inside a word (\`Se\*Privilege\`), \`TERM()\` of part of a longer term and \`CASE()\` of a word with a wildcard inside it match as on the original lines. \- \`tx\` and \`txf\` expand an event whose values begin or end with white space or a carriage return, such as a Windows event with CR LF line ends, to its full text, and a carriage return inside an event comes back in place. \- \`tx\` expands events whose template appears twice in the indexers' copy of the template collection. An event \`tx\` cannot expand keeps its compact text and says why in \`tenx_expand_refused\`. \- The Consume KV search stores every template record indexed since the last one it stored, a burst of new templates included, and its first run after an install or an upgrade reads every template record in the index. \`tx\` and \`txf\` warn when Consume KV failed, is still loading, or has not run for fifteen minutes. \- Alerts compiled in the Compile Alert view find their events when the scheduler runs them, including events of templates whose hash contains \`$\`. The recompile pass rewrites alerts compiled with an earlier version within 15 minutes of the upgrade, unless someone has edited them since. \- An epoch-seconds timestamp with a fraction, such as \`msg\=audit(1723042099.699:13369)\`, expands as written and sets the event's time. \- Beside a heavy forwarder, the Receiver can write compact events to files that the heavy forwarder reads and sends to the indexers with its own outputs, with no HTTP Event Collector or token. The \`\_indexers\` package gives each event back its host, source, index and time, and field maps run on the heavy forwarder. \- \`tx\` expands the events a FortiGate field map leaves under the compact sourcetype, such as FortiGate lines the add-on does not type, and a field map keeps the time of an event marked \`tenx_time\=sender\`. \- \`tx\` and \`txf\` run inside \`| union \[...]\`, in a search, a dashboard panel and a saved search, as they do inside \`multisearch\`, \`append\` and \`join\`. \- A search that holds more than one \`tx\` or \`txf\`, such as two arms of a \`multisearch\` or \`union\`, finds every event of each arm. \- \`| tx\` and \`| tenxsearch\` return their events inside \`append\`, \`join\` and \`union\`, and an unexpected error shows on the search instead of an empty result. \- Requires the Log10x Receiver at release 1.1.181 or later and Splunk Enterprise 9.4 through 10.6. After upgrading where a field map is installed, give the role of the token \`activate\` and \`check\` use search access to \`\_internal\`, and schedule \`check\` every minute. A map that \`gen\` generates again after the upgrade can carry a new index-time rule; install both of its apps again whole before running \`activate\`.


Short Description:
Send Splunk the logs that sampling and filters keep out to fit the license, on that same license. Compact events take a fraction of the volume and expand back byte-identical at search time; classic dashboards keep their SPL, and one command covers the search bar, saved searches, alerts and the REST API.


Description:
With the Log10x App, Splunk can index compact log events and still search, chart and alert on the original lines. The 10x Receiver stores each event as a template hash plus the values that change, so a stream of repeated patterns takes less of the license. On the OpenTelemetry demo, Splunk's license meter counted 63.91% fewer bytes, encoded events and templates included, and every line expanded back byte-identical with the Receiver settings in the installation steps (measurement: https://github.com/log-10x/benchmarks/tree/main/splunk-license). The same license then holds more: sources that were sampled, filtered or kept out of Splunk to stay under the limit can come back, or the license can be smaller. To search by what the lines say, write the tx macro in front of an ordinary search: index=my_index `tx` "payment failed" NOT retry. It runs as native SPL in the search bar, Dashboard Studio, saved searches and alerts, and NOT, OR, groups, phrases, field conditions, and values such as IP addresses and hostnames behave as they do on the original data. Classic dashboards keep their SPL: the browser sends each panel's search to the app, which rewrites it on the server. An alert created in the app's Compile Alert view is compiled once into a native saved search. The 10x Receiver produces compact events, and it is free on up to 10 nodes (https://www.log10x.com/pricing). No sign-up is required: with no license token it runs the full product on up to 10 nodes, air-gapped, with no expiry (https://doc.log10x.com/manage/license/). The app itself is open source under the MIT license.

item.title: Riskability - v1.5.1 [Version Update]
item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
# Riskability 1.5.1 What changed since 1.4.1, the version on Splunkbase today. Grouped by what you will notice, not by commit. Nothing has been removed that you were using. ## In one paragraph 1.5.1 adds an Executive summary page that prints as three A4 landscape sheets, a count of new findings that opens the list behind it, and rebuilds the Routes page around the question it was always meant to answer: of the jumps the firewall has seen, which could an attacker actually take, and how far. Every jump is now graded by what taking it would need, a crash-only flaw no longer counts as a way in, and the graph is walked once an hour so it draws an estate of thousands. It also fixes a Routes page where every click said "No results found", and a Feed administration page that looked idle while an import was most of the way through. ## New: Executive summary A page for the people who ask how exposed the organisation is, in the order they ask it: known exploited vulnerabilities open, of those how many answer the network, systems with an open vulnerability, risks consciously accepted, how long serious findings stay open, and how far to trust the figures. Then the reachability matrix, the severity ring, thirty days of movement and the five things to fix first. Every figure is the linked page's own query against the same hourly roll-ups, so a number here always matches the page it links to. There is no composite score, because the app cannot defend one. Print or save as PDF. Splunk's Export to PDF leaves out every custom chart, and an air-gapped search head has no server-side renderer, so the page prints in the reader's own browser: three landscape sheets, always the same shape, with the charts redrawn as vector graphics in a light palette so they stay sharp at any size. Checked in Chromium-based browsers and in Safari; in Safari, pick landscape in the print dialog. ## New: a count of new findings, and the list behind it Start here has a New findings tile: open findings first reported in the last seven days, accepted risks left out, at every confidence. Click the number and Findings opens on those findings, through two new filters, First reported (24 hours, 7 days, 30 days or any time) and Accepted risks (shown or hidden), and a First reported column. New means the first time the app reported the finding, not when the host's inventory was collected. A feed update that flags software nobody has touched in months produces findings that are new today, and those are the ones this tile exists for. Findings recorded before this release have no such date and count by their inventory date instead, which is never later than the truth, so nothing old is passed off as new. ## Routes: graded by what an attacker would need A permitted flow is a path, not an exploit, and the page used to draw every jump the same way, coloured by known-exploited and EPSS, which say nothing about whether a flaw can be reached over this wire. Every jump is now graded from the CVSS vectors of the findings open on the listener it lands on: * CVE-enabled, solid red: reachable over the network, with no account and no user action, and a high impact on confidentiality or integrity. That is the shape of code execution, an authentication bypass or stolen secrets. * Needs a foothold, solid amber: reachable, but it wants credentials or a click. * Unrated, dashed amber: an open finding has no CVSS vector, so the app cannot say. * Permitted only, dashed grey: nothing usable over the network is open there, so the jump needs a zero-day or permissions. A flaw whose only impact is availability opens no jump. CVE-2024-0760 in BIND, a TCP flood that makes the server unstable while it lasts, can crash the listener but cannot put anyone on the host, and neither can HTTP/2 Rapid Reset, so a DNS or web server carrying only those is not drawn as a way in. A low impact alone, a minor leak or change, does not open one either. The findings panel says which of these each CVE is, in an "Over the wire" column: no foothold needed, needs credentials or a click, only to take it down, only a minor leak or change. Every host an attacker can reach from an entry point on CVE-enabled jumps alone is ringed red. A new table lists every path from an entry point, worst first: how many jumps, how far the CVE-only stretch goes, the jump where it stops, and the CVEs behind each jump. The software is on the jump. Each jump is labelled with its protocol, the port it landed on and the software listening there, the first jump from an entry point included. Hovering a jump lists every port it was seen on and what is open behind each, and clicking it opens the findings on those ports rather than the whole host's. ## Routes: drawn at estate size The page used to walk the graph inside its own search on every load, which worked on fifteen hosts and would have taken minutes on five thousand, and hit a limits.conf ceiling before that without saying so. An hourly job now walks it once, with a breadth-first search in a dedicated search command, and the page reads the result. It opens on CVE-enabled jumps and twenty-five hosts per hop, keeps the worst, and says how many it left out. Paths are capped by the job, two thousand at most, and every row says when a cap cut the list. The panel grows with the densest hop instead of packing a large graph into 640 pixels, and a panel resized in the dashboard editor redraws at its new height without a reload. ## Fixed Every click on the Routes graph said "No results found". The click reported its kind with the column prefix still on it, and the findings search compared that against the bare kind. Every edge tooltip on Routes read "N CVEs through this hop" with N being the session count. The label and class were built and then dropped before the chart drew them. Feed administration looked idle during an import. The staged-bundles list redraws every few seconds, and the bundle being imported came back each time with a fresh Import button, so it read as "nothing started" while the import was most of the way through. That bundle now says it is importing and cannot be deleted mid-import, no other bundle can start an import until it finishes, and the percentage counts advisories as well as ranges, so it no longer sits at 99 percent for the whole advisory phase. Explain in depth was refused on Splunk Free. Free has no access control and reports no capabilities for anyone, which the AI page read as "not allowed". On a licensed Splunk the riskability_ai_explain capability decides, exactly as before. On a CVE's page, "Matching hosts in this fleet" came seventh, after five panels of feed text. It now follows the headline figures directly.


Short Description:
Correlate the software your fleet already reports against offline CVE databases on a search head with no internet access. Ranks findings by exploitation likelihood and by whether the network can actually reach them. Track software that is already or soon becoming End Of Life!


Description:
Most vulnerability tooling cannot run where it is needed most. A search head with no route to the internet cannot call an API, pull a feed on a schedule or fetch a score on demand. Riskability is built for that machine. It takes the software inventory your hosts already report, correlates it against databases you carry across the air gap yourself, and answers what a CVE count never does: of everything found, what should somebody do tonight? CVSS says how bad a flaw would be if exploited, not how likely that is, and never whether your copy is reachable. WHAT THIS APP ADDS Exploitation likelihood. Findings are ranked by EPSS, the published probability of exploitation in the wild, and by the CISA KEV catalogue of vulnerabilities already exploited. Both arrive in the feed you import, never fetched live. Reachability, measured on the host. The collector reports listening ports and the process behind each, so findings answering a network address are separated from those answering only loopback or nothing. On a test fleet that turned 10,206 open findings into 11 that answer the network. It reorders the work. It never shortens it. Reachability, observed at the boundary. With your firewall logs in Splunk, the app can also say whether a permitted flow from the internet or an admin network has actually reached a port, and draw the jumps from entry point to the findings at the end. A site without firewall logs loses nothing. End of support. A CVE says a thing is broken; end of support says nobody will fix it again, which no advisory states. The app names software with no supported release. Rules your fleet needs. A risk the scoring signals cannot see can be written as a rule raising a finding one tier. Rules ship off, and a replay shows what each would move first. Optional AI explanation. A model on your own hardware writes the reasoning beside each finding: why it ranks where it does, what to do, which ATT&CK techniques apply. The score is arithmetic from measured facts and the model cannot change it. Where an answer contradicts the evidence, the row says so. WHAT IT REFUSES TO GUESS Every finding carries a confidence level describing the evidence, not the severity. A distribution that backports fixes without changing the version is reported as informational rather than asserted. A Coverage dashboard lists what the data cannot speak to, because a gap in visibility is not an absence of risk. Accepted risks go to an audit index written once, never rewritten. NO UNINTENTIONAL DATA OUT Nothing goes out unless you set up AI, and the recommended shape is a model in the same location as this Splunk instance, so nothing leaves the organisation. You build a feed bundle on a connected machine, carry it across and import it.

Paste the vendor's documentation and Chuka writes the collector, then lists anything the documentation does not say. - One tested collector engine: API keys, basic, bearer, OAuth client credentials, OAuth with a one-time sign-in and client certificates, with every common paging style, new events only, duplicates removed and rate limits honoured. - A collector turns on only after it passes a test on the real API, including a restart that must lose and repeat nothing. Credentials go only to the host they were entered for. - Runs on the search head, one cluster member at a time, or on a heavy forwarder. Health, field changes and failures are shown and alerted, and a collector running in two places is caught. - One add-on gives the ad hoc search head the same fields, CIM mapping and tags as the Enterprise Security search head. **Parsing Studio** - CSV logs with no header line: every column in its place, named in place or from the vendor's documented layout, and deployed so a quoted comma stays in one field. - A deployment that fails part way is undone, and a rollback restores what was there before. **Scale and reliability** - Scans grow with the size of the estate, not its square. Tested on a model estate of 10,000 sourcetypes and 5,000 saved searches. - Background reads return every row, and large scans are kept compressed, so later visits open at once. - An alert fires again when a fault comes back, and a mass failure arrives as one message. - Two people working on one issue no longer overwrite each other. **Trust** - A Vyrux admin manages the licence, connectors and proxy without a Splunk admin role. - Field settings Chuka writes are never run as searches. Evidence and the Vyrux log are protected from change by members. **A calmer, consistent console** - One main button style, one date format, one colour scale for scores, readable banners, text on one type scale, and help on every figure. - Every word reviewed: true statements only, empty states and errors that say what to do next, and one term for one thing. The full guide, with every change in this release: https://vyrux-docs.pages.dev


Short Description:
Know that your Splunk works. Prove your logs arrive, your rules can fire and your ATT&CK coverage is real, then fix every gap.


Description:
Every SOC pays for its logs and writes its detections. Few can show, on any given morning, that the logs arrived, that the parsing still holds and that the correlation searches they rely on can still fire. That gap stays hidden until an incident review finds it. Vyrux closes it inside your own Splunk. Every 15 minutes it checks each log, each rule and each ATT&CK technique you count as covered. It explains what broke, traces it to its root cause and turns it into owned work, with a fix your engineers test before anything changes in Splunk. Chuka, the built-in AI detection engineer, explains, fixes and drafts rules from your real fields, and Splunk checks everything Chuka writes before anyone can use it. Vyrux is one app on the search head, including the Enterprise Security search head. It is not SaaS. It reads Splunk with each person's own permissions, keeps its records in your KV store, and your log data stays with you.

item.description:
Platform: Splunk


Release Notes:
* Three detection types: **Detection**, **Alert** and **Endpoint**. `category` is `Detection`, `Alert` or `Endpoint`, and `detection_type` is `detection`, `alert` or `endpoint`. * Reads the type from the new `cynamics.type` field and maps events already indexed in the same way, so the dashboard and searches cover old and new events. * `Agent Detection` and `AI Detection` are now `Detection`, and `Endpoint Detection` is now `Endpoint`. Saved searches and alerts on the old values need updating. * The data input’s Detection types are `detection`, `alert` and `endpoint`. Inputs set up with an earlier version keep working unchanged


Short Description:
Parses Cynamics AI NDR detections (sourcetype cynamics:detection) and maps them to the CIM Intrusion Detection and Alerts data models. Includes an overview dashboard, and a data input that pulls the detections from the Cynamics API.


Description:
The Cynamics AI NDR Add-on brings Cynamics AI NDR detections into Splunk Enterprise and Splunk Cloud Platform as first-class security events. It parses the cynamics:detection sourcetype and maps each detection to the Common Information Model's Intrusion Detection and Alerts data models, so Splunk Enterprise Security and other CIM-based apps see Cynamics detections next to your other intrusion detections and alerts. Detections arrive either from Cynamics, which sends them to your HTTP Event Collector, or from the add-on's data input, which pulls them from the Cynamics API with an API key, for a Splunk that Cynamics can't reach. An overview dashboard and an Open in Cynamics action take analysts from a detection to its page in Cynamics.
